title: Rafael and the Harvest
premise: Folklorist Yara Voss arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to record harvest songs that locals refuse to sing twice, only to discover that every photograph from her grandmother's house now contains an extra empty chair — a chair that appears in rooms she enters, waiting. The chair belonged to someone taken by the village in 1974, when her grandmother helped feed a neighbor to the field-spirit in exchange for a good harvest, and the spirit has been holding its debt ever since, collecting memories as interest. As Yara uncovers the 1974 pact through corrupted tape recordings and the half-erased memories of the last surviving elders, she realizes the spirit wants not a substitute but a return: what was stolen must be given back before the harvest moon rises. In the end, Yara returns the dead woman's name — which the village took and never spoke again — restoring her to memory at the cost of the villagers' own recollections of their loved ones, and the chair finally fills with someone the living can no longer remember but Yara alone will carry forward.
about_author: Felix Okonkwo is a Nigerian-British writer who spent three years documenting oral traditions across rural Europe before turning those recordings into fiction. He writes horror rooted in folklore, believing the scariest stories are the ones communities agree never to repeat.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Yara arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and her grandmother's old letters, eager to document the harvest songs. An elderly innkeeper sings one verse for her, then goes pale and refuses to continue. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease as she notices every villager glances at an empty corner of the taproom.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting photographs in her grandmother's abandoned house, Yara finds that every image — even ones from decades ago — now shows a plain wooden chair where none was photographed. Her camera's new photos develop the same way. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: rational denial cracking; documentation begins to feel less like scholarship and more like being watched.

chapters.title: What the Field Remembers
chapters.summary: Yara interviews Tomas, the oldest farmer, who describes the miraculous harvest of 1974 and then cannot recall his own wife's face mid-sentence. He weeps without knowing why. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief without object — the first evidence that memories are being eaten.

chapters.title: The Chair Follows
chapters.summary: Yara wakes at 3 a.m. to find the wooden chair standing in her bedroom, facing her bed, though she locked the door. It is warm, like something recently sat there. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into resolve; she decides to treat the chair as evidence rather than flee.

chapters.title: Tape Side B
chapters.summary: In her grandmother's effects, Yara finds a reel-to-reel tape labeled 1974. Halfway through a harvest song, the audio warps into a second voice beneath the melody — a woman singing words that don't belong to any known dialect. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: scholarly excitement giving way to dread as she recognizes the voice asking, politely, to be remembered.

chapters.title: The Village That Agreed
chapters.summary: Yara confronts the innkeeper with the tape; the woman confesses fragments: in 1974 the village made a bargain during a famine year, and everyone consented, and everyone forgot on purpose. She begs Yara to leave. POV: alternating Yara and the innkeeper's fractured recollection. Emotional beat: complicity — the horror is communal, not supernatural alone.

chapters.title: Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: In the church archive Yara finds the parish register: one page from autumn 1974 has been razored out, but the binding ghost shows the impression of a name. She makes a rubbing. The letters won't photograph. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by the sense that the name is resisting being found.

chapters.title: Marta
chapters.summary: A middle-aged woman Yara has never met greets her by name and says, 'You have her chin.' She is Marta, daughter of the woman who vanished in 1974 — except Marta cannot say her mother's name, only describe an absence shaped like a person. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: a lifetime of unexplained mourning finally given a shape.

chapters.title: Interest Accrued
chapters.summary: Yara catalogs the village's losses: elders who've forgotten their children's names, a man who re-grieves his dead son fresh each morning. The spirit hasn't just held its debt — it has been feeding. POV: Yara, interwoven with transcribed testimonies. Emotional beat: cold anger replacing fear; this is predation dressed as tradition.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Confession
chapters.summary: A sealed letter, to be opened 'when the chair comes,' reveals Yara's grandmother helped choose the victim — a lonely outsider nobody would miss — and took payment: her family would never hunger. Yara's own comfortable childhood was bought here. POV: Yara reading. Emotional beat: shame and inheritance; the debt runs through her blood.

chapters.title: They Start Remembering Wrong
chapters.summary: As the moon waxes, villagers begin recalling the missing woman — but as a monster, a thief, a reason the sacrifice was justified. The spirit is rewriting the story to keep its meal. POV: multiple villagers in chorus. Emotional beat: horror of narrative itself; memory weaponized against the truth.

chapters.title: The Rubbing Speaks
chapters.summary: Working the name-impression by candlelight, Yara hears the letters whispered aloud: Ilse Brandt. The chair in her room turns to face the door, as if listening. That night it sits beside her bed, occupied — by warmth, by an indentation, by presence. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: communion with the dead; fear braided with tenderness.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Ilse's presence communicates through dreams and tape warp: the village didn't give her to the field — they stole her from it after she'd already been promised, taking back the harvest but keeping the price unpaid. The spirit isn't cruel; it is owed. POV: Yara dreaming. Emotional beat: moral inversion — the monster may be the wronged party.

chapters.title: The Elders' Council
chapters.summary: Yara presents everything to the village's remaining leaders. Some deny; some break down; one, the innkeeper's brother, admits he was a boy who watched and was made to forget. They vote — barely — to help her return the name. POV: ensemble. Emotional beat: reluctant collective courage; a community choosing to unmake its founding lie.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Two landowners whose prosperity descends from the pact burn Yara's tapes and lock her out of the archive. The chair appears in their homes that night, and by morning one has forgotten his own name entirely. POV: shifting between Yara and the saboteurs. Emotional beat: escalating stakes — the debt collects faster as the moon fills.

chapters.title: Relearning Ilse
chapters.summary: Marta and Yara reconstruct Ilse from fragments: a photograph hidden in a hymnal, a recipe in her hand, Marta's body-memory of being carried. They practice speaking her name until it stops feeling like a wound. POV: Marta and Yara. Emotional beat: grief transformed into restoration; love as research.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Harvest eve. The village gathers in the taproom where the song was first sung twice. Yara teaches them Ilse's verse from the warped tape. Half sing; half cover their ears. The chairs in every house scrape toward their doors. POV: ensemble. Emotional beat: terrible anticipation; a whole community holding its breath.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Under the full moon, Yara walks into the field carrying the register page, the tape, and Ilse's name spoken aloud. The crops part around a figure seated in the chair — Ilse, worn thin as paper. The spirit rises from the soil to collect. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: awe and terror fused; the climax of reckoning.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Yara offers not a substitute but restitution: the name returned to every mouth, the record restored, the village's claim on silence broken. The spirit demands the equivalent weight in memory — and takes the villagers' recollections of their own beloved dead, leaving them grieving without knowing for whom. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: sacrificial clarity; justice that still costs everything.

chapters.title: Empty Chairs, Full Field
chapters.summary: Dawn. The harvest is over; the fields stand bare and honest. Villagers wander their kitchens touching chairs they can't explain crying over. Marta remembers her mother fully — the only one who does — because Yara gave her own share of memory to keep Ilse intact. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: bittersweet restoration; one whole memory purchased with many hollowed ones.

chapters.title: What Documentation Is For
chapters.summary: Yara finishes her monograph, but instead of publishing, she deposits it with Marta: Ilse's name, life, and theft written down so no bargain can ever unwrite them again. She understands at last that documentation was always prayer — a promise to carry what others cannot. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: quiet purpose; the theme resolved into vocation.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Leaving Hollowmere, Yara pauses at the field's edge and sings the harvest song through, then — deliberately — begins it again. Nothing stops her. Behind her, faintly, a second voice joins on the second verse. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: release and haunting entwined; some debts end not with payment but with witness.
